front: Name the usual preprocessing steps in order
back: Normalise (case, Unicode), tokenise, optionally drop stop words, optionally stem or lemmatise.
Stemming chops suffixes by rules (fast, may give non-words like poni). Lemmatisation uses a lexicon and part of speech to return the dictionary form (ran -> run).

front: Why is defining a word hard?
back: Compounds (pomme de terre), clitics (aujourd'hui, don't), German compounds, URLs and hashtags: whitespace is not a reliable boundary.
Special tokens: <UNK> stands for words outside the vocabulary, <PAD> pads sequences to a common length.
$X\in\mathbb{N}^{N\times|V|}$, entry = count of token $j$ in document $d$. Order is discarded.
A document uses few distinct tokens out of $|V|$ (often $10^4$-$10^6$), so most entries are zero; store (row, col, value).
Self-information of seeing the token in a document: ubiquitous words carry little, rare words carry much; the log keeps the scale tame.
Removes the effect of document length and turns cosine similarity into a plain dot product.
$\frac{a\cdot b}{\|a\|\|b\|}$, between 0 and 1 for non-negative vectors; the angle, not the length.

front: What does an n-gram add to a bag of words?
back: Local order: bigrams such as not_good become features, at the cost of up to $|V|^n$ possible features.

front: Where must the vectoriser be fitted?
back: On the training split only; reuse its vocabulary and IDF on validation and test to avoid leakage.

front: Main limitation of sparse count vectors
back: No notion of meaning: car and automobile are unrelated columns. Dense embeddings address this.

front: When is removing stop words harmful?
back: When small words carry the signal, e.g. removing not in sentiment analysis.
